evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The document is NCHS Data Brief No. 480, titled 'Long COVID in Adults: United States, 2022,' and its tables and text report exclusively on Long COVID prevalence from the 2022 National Health Interview Survey; there is no mention of Lyme disease anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a CDC/NCHS Data Brief (No. 480, September 2023) using 2022 National Health Interview Survey data to report what percentage of U.S. adults ever had or currently have Long COVID, defined as self-reported symptoms lasting 3+ months after a positive test or doctor-diagnosed COVID-19. It breaks these percentages down by sex, age group, race/Hispanic origin, family income relative to the federal poverty level, and urbanization level. The document reports prevalence only - it contains no dollar costs, treatment costs, productivity-loss, caregiving-time, or insurance-access figures. Women, adults ages 35-49, and adults in more rural areas showed higher prevalence of both 'ever' and 'current' Long COVID, while Asian adults and higher-income adults (400%+ FPL) showed lower prevalence.

contextual_issues: The document states Long COVID 'can lead to long-term health and economic impacts on those affected and on society,' citing an external JAMA Health Forum paper (ref 2), but does not itself quantify any medical cost, non-medical cost, productivity loss, caregiving time, or financial consequence.

A figure that 77.5% of people ages 16+ had COVID-19 antibodies as of December 2022 is mentioned in the Summary, but this is explicitly attributed to the CDC COVID Data Tracker / Nationwide Blood Donor Seroprevalence Survey (ref 3), not derived or adopted by this document's own NHIS analysis, and it measures prior infection, not Long COVID.
No mention is made in this document of diagnostic delay, repeated care-seeking, insurance or access barriers, or direct/indirect cost categories for Long COVID.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, non-medical cost, or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported; cost modeling would require a separate linked economic dataset (e.g., MEPS or claims data) not present in this document.
No data on diagnostic delay, number of care encounters, or insurance/access barriers for Long COVID patients.

This is a single cross-sectional year (2022); no duration, persistence-over-time, or multi-year trend data are reported, so lifetime or multi-year burden cannot be derived without an explicitly labeled extrapolation assumption.

Race/ethnicity breakdown excludes non-Hispanic adults of races other than Asian, Black, and White 'due to the inability to make statistically reliable estimates' (though these adults are included in total estimates), limiting the completeness of that subgroup disaggregation.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool 'ever Long COVID' and 'current Long COVID' percentages together - 'current' is a nested subset of 'ever' (ever symptoms plus symptoms still present at interview), not an independent additive measure.

Do not pool this NHIS 2022 self-report cross-sectional prevalence estimate with any claims-based, EHR-coded (e.g., U09.9), or other survey-wave (e.g., Household Pulse Survey) Long COVID prevalence estimate - different case definitions, data sources, and time periods.

Do not extrapolate the 2022 single-year national prevalence percentages to other calendar years or to a lifetime risk estimate without explicitly labeling this as an assumption/projection, since the document provides only one year of data.

Race/Hispanic-origin breakdown in this document excludes non-Hispanic adults of races other than Asian, Black, and White from the shown subgroup estimates (for reliability reasons) while still including them in the total/pooled estimate - the pooled total and the shown subgroup estimates are not fully reconcilable as a closed set.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Women were more likely than men to ever have Long COVID (8.5% vs. 5.2%) and more likely to currently have Long COVID (4.4% vs. 2.3%) in 2022 (both differences significant at p<0.05 per the document's own test).

crosscheck_candidates.label: Percentage of U.S. adults who ever had Long COVID
crosscheck_candidates.definition: Self-reported symptoms lasting 3 months or longer not present prior to COVID-19, among adults reporting a positive test or doctor's diagnosis of COVID-19 and symptomatic; NHIS 2022 Sample Adult interview.

crosscheck_candidates.label: Percentage of U.S. adults currently experiencing Long COVID
crosscheck_candidates.definition: Meets ever-Long-COVID definition plus presence of symptoms at time of interview; NHIS 2022 Sample Adult interview.

decision_relevance.summary: This document supplies population-level prevalence benchmarks (not cost data) that could help patients/advocates understand how common Long COVID is within their demographic group, help care delivery teams identify higher-prevalence subpopulations (women, adults 35-49, nonmetropolitan residents) for screening or outreach prioritization, and help payers/policymakers estimate the relative size of affected subpopulations for 2022. Any economic simulator built from this document alone would need to source cost-per-case, treatment-utilization, or productivity-loss data from elsewhere, since none is reported here. The demographic breakdowns are useful for equity-focused resource targeting given CDC's own protected-category framing (sex, age, race/ethnicity, income, urbanization).
use_cases: Policy or payer analysts can use the sex/age/race/income/urbanization prevalence breakdowns to estimate the relative size of affected adult subpopulations in 2022 for planning purposes, while sourcing cost-per-case data separately since this document reports no cost figures.

Care delivery teams can use the higher-prevalence subgroups identified here (women, adults ages 35-49, nonmetropolitan/rural residents) to prioritize screening, outreach, or clinical-capacity planning for Long COVID.

contextual_issues: The document states Long COVID 'can lead to long-term health and economic impacts on those affected and on society,' citing an external JAMA Health Forum paper (ref 2), but does not itself quantify any medical cost, non-medical cost, productivity loss, caregiving time, or financial consequence.

A figure that 77.5% of people ages 16+ had COVID-19 antibodies as of December 2022 is mentioned in the Summary, but this is explicitly attributed to the CDC COVID Data Tracker / Nationwide Blood Donor Seroprevalence Survey (ref 3), not derived or adopted by this document's own NHIS analysis, and it measures prior infection, not Long COVID.
No mention is made in this document of diagnostic delay, repeated care-seeking, insurance or access barriers, or direct/indirect cost categories for Long COVID.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, non-medical cost, or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported; cost modeling would require a separate linked economic dataset (e.g., MEPS or claims data) not present in this document.
No data on diagnostic delay, number of care encounters, or insurance/access barriers for Long COVID patients.

This is a single cross-sectional year (2022); no duration, persistence-over-time, or multi-year trend data are reported, so lifetime or multi-year burden cannot be derived without an explicitly labeled extrapolation assumption.

Race/ethnicity breakdown excludes non-Hispanic adults of races other than Asian, Black, and White 'due to the inability to make statistically reliable estimates' (though these adults are included in total estimates), limiting the completeness of that subgroup disaggregation.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool 'ever Long COVID' and 'current Long COVID' percentages together - 'current' is a nested subset of 'ever' (ever symptoms plus symptoms still present at interview), not an independent additive measure.

Do not pool this NHIS 2022 self-report cross-sectional prevalence estimate with any claims-based, EHR-coded (e.g., U09.9), or other survey-wave (e.g., Household Pulse Survey) Long COVID prevalence estimate - different case definitions, data sources, and time periods.

Do not extrapolate the 2022 single-year national prevalence percentages to other calendar years or to a lifetime risk estimate without explicitly labeling this as an assumption/projection, since the document provides only one year of data.

Race/Hispanic-origin breakdown in this document excludes non-Hispanic adults of races other than Asian, Black, and White from the shown subgroup estimates (for reliability reasons) while still including them in the total/pooled estimate - the pooled total and the shown subgroup estimates are not fully reconcilable as a closed set.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Women were more likely than men to ever have Long COVID (8.5% vs. 5.2%) and more likely to currently have Long COVID (4.4% vs. 2.3%) in 2022 (both differences significant at p<0.05 per the document's own test).

decision_relevance.summary: This document supplies population-level prevalence benchmarks (not cost data) that could help patients/advocates understand how common Long COVID is within their demographic group, help care delivery teams identify higher-prevalence subpopulations (women, adults 35-49, nonmetropolitan residents) for screening or outreach prioritization, and help payers/policymakers estimate the relative size of affected subpopulations for 2022. Any economic simulator built from this document alone would need to source cost-per-case, treatment-utilization, or productivity-loss data from elsewhere, since none is reported here. The demographic breakdowns are useful for equity-focused resource targeting given CDC's own protected-category framing (sex, age, race/ethnicity, income, urbanization).
use_cases: Policy or payer analysts can use the sex/age/race/income/urbanization prevalence breakdowns to estimate the relative size of affected adult subpopulations in 2022 for planning purposes, while sourcing cost-per-case data separately since this document reports no cost figures.

Care delivery teams can use the higher-prevalence subgroups identified here (women, adults ages 35-49, nonmetropolitan/rural residents) to prioritize screening, outreach, or clinical-capacity planning for Long COVID.

package.documentation:
## Source
This simulator is built entirely from CDC/NCHS Data Brief No. 480, *Long COVID in Adults: United States, 2022* (September 2023), based on the 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Long COVID is defined in the source as self-reported symptoms lasting 3 months or longer, not present before infection, among adults reporting a positive test or clinician diagnosis of COVID-19.

## What is modeled
All inputs are subgroup prevalence percentages the document reports directly (sex, age, urbanization), each labeled with its 2022 data period and 'observed' evidence status. All outputs are simple subtraction gaps between two subgroup prevalence figures, with each output's label stating directly what a positive versus negative value means. These are descriptive comparisons, not causal estimates - the document reports that the sex gap is statistically significant (p<0.05) but does not explain why any of these gaps exist.

## What is NOT modeled
This document reports prevalence only. It contains no dollar costs, treatment costs, productivity loss, caregiving time, or insurance/access-barrier data, so no cost or payer field is attached to any output here, and total expenditures cannot be derived from this simulator. Any economic burden estimate would require a separate linked dataset (e.g., MEPS or claims data), which this document does not provide.

## Key comparison boundaries
'Current' Long COVID prevalence (3.4% nationally) is a nested subset of 'ever' Long COVID prevalence (6.9% nationally), not an independent or additive figure - the two should never be summed. This is a single cross-sectional year (2022); the document provides no multi-year trend or lifetime-risk data, so figures should not be extrapolated to other years without explicitly labeling that as an assumption. The race/Hispanic-origin breakdown in the source excludes non-Hispanic adults of races other than Asian, Black, and White from its subgroup figures (for reliability reasons) while still including them in the pooled national total; that subgroup detail is not reproduced in this simulator.

## Sex/gender findings
The document reports women had significantly higher ever-Long-COVID prevalence (8.5% vs. 5.2% for men) and current-Long-COVID prevalence (4.4% vs. 2.3% for men) in 2022; both sex-specific gaps are preserved as separate inputs and outputs here rather than pooled into a single figure.

## Exploration ranges
All input min/max ranges (0-15%) are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not values specified by the source document.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Percentage of U.S. adults who ever had Long COVID (2022): the document reports 6.9% as the share of all U.S. adults that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 7 wave(s) in that period ranged from 14% to 14.8% (interval bounds 13.4% to 15.4%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Percentage of U.S. adults currently experiencing Long COVID (2022): the document reports 3.4% as the share of all U.S. adults that currently have Long COVID; the national survey's 7 wave(s) in that period ranged from 5.8% to 7.6% (interval bounds 5.5% to 8.1%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
